summary: Describes the Sun RPC version 2 message protocol that Sun Microsystems and others used for remote procedure calls, proposed for the Internet's consideration. It was not an Internet standard. It replaces RFC 1050.

eli5.summary: It lets one computer ask another to run a task, like calling a helper in another room and getting the answer back.

subtitle: How Sun's RPC lets a program on one machine call a procedure on another, and what the call and reply messages look like.

tldr.problem: Programs on different machines need a common way to call procedures on each other, identify the procedure, match replies to calls and prove who is calling.
tldr.mechanism: Version 2 of Sun's RPC message protocol defines call and reply messages in XDR. A call names a program, version and procedure and carries credentials and a verifier. The reply says whether the call was accepted and what happened.
tldr.outcome: It is a description of a protocol Sun and others were using, offered for the Internet's consideration. It is not an Internet standard, and it replaces RFC 1050.

today: RFC 1057 is an Informational memo from June 1988 and is not an Internet standard. It replaces RFC 1050, and the unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What Sun RPC Specifies
sections.content:
RFC 1057 specifies version two of the message protocol used in Sun's Remote Procedure Call (RPC) package. The messages are described in the XDR (eXternal Data Representation) language, and the RFC assumes the reader already knows XDR. It does not try to justify RPC systems or describe how they are used.

The status section is plain: Sun Microsystems and others are using this protocol, and it is proposed for the Internet's consideration. The memo is not an Internet standard at this time.
sections.eli5: This document is the rulebook for how computers send each other 'please run this job' notes and the answers back.

sections.title: The RPC Model and Its Limits
sections.content:
Each call has two sides: an active client that sends a call, and a server that sends back a reply. A network service is a collection of one or more remote programs, and each program offers one or more remote procedures. A server may support several versions of a program so that it stays compatible as protocols change. The words client and server only apply to a single transaction, so one machine can play both roles at different times.

The model resembles a local procedure call: the caller sends a call message carrying the parameters, waits, and resumes when the reply carries the results. The RFC says this is only an example. The protocol puts no limits on concurrency, so calls may be asynchronous, or a server may start a separate task for each incoming call.

The RFC lists four ways a remote call differs from a local one: failures of the server or network must be handled, hidden arguments cannot be passed as global variables or side effects, remote procedures usually run one or more orders of magnitude slower, and authentication may be needed on insecure networks.

Binding a client to a service is not part of the protocol. The RFC compares RPC to the jump-subroutine instruction of a network: binding software makes it useful, and may itself use RPC.
sections.eli5: Asking someone in another room is not the same as doing it yourself: they might not answer, it takes longer, and you may need to show who you are.

sections.title: Call and Reply Messages
sections.content:
Every message starts with a transaction identifier, xid, followed by a two-armed union whose discriminant is msg_type: CALL (0) or REPLY (1). The xid of a reply always matches the call. It is only for clients matching replies to calls, or servers spotting retransmissions. A server must not treat it as a sequence number.

A call body carries rpcvers (which must equal 2), then prog, vers and proc, which uniquely name the procedure. Next come two authentication fields, cred and verf, followed by the procedure's own parameters.

A reply is either accepted (MSG_ACCEPTED) or denied (MSG_DENIED). An accepted reply starts with a verifier the server uses to validate itself to the client, then a status. The status is SUCCESS with the results, or an error such as PROG_UNAVAIL, PROG_MISMATCH (which returns the lowest and highest supported versions), PROC_UNAVAIL or GARBAGE_ARGS. A call is denied with RPC_MISMATCH (the RPC version is not 2, so the supported range is returned) or AUTH_ERROR.

Program numbers are handed out in blocks of hexadecimal 20000000. The first block, 0 to 1fffffff, is defined by Sun, the second is for user-defined programs, and the third is transient, for programs that generate numbers dynamically. The rest are reserved.
sections.eli5: A call note says which helper, which job and who is asking. The answer note says 'done, here is the result' or tells you what went wrong.

sections.title: Authentication Flavors
sections.content:
Each call carries a credential and verifier, and each reply carries a response verifier. All three have the same shape: an opaque_auth, which is an auth_flavor followed by an opaque body of up to 400 bytes. The RPC layer does not interpret the body. Separate authentication protocols define what it means.

The RFC defines three flavors. AUTH_NULL (0) is for calls where the client does not know its identity or the server does not care. AUTH_UNIX (1) sends a stamp, the machine name, the user and group IDs and a list of groups. It has no real verifier, so the RFC notes that credentials can easily be faked. A server can reply with AUTH_SHORT (2), a shorthand credential the client may use instead.

AUTH_DES (3) addresses the weaknesses of UNIX authentication. Clients are named by a network name (a netname such as unix.515@sun.com). The verifier is mainly an encrypted timestamp, which only a client that knows the session's conversation key can produce. The client generates that DES key and sends it in the first call, encrypted with Diffie-Hellman using 192-bit keys. The client and server need a shared notion of time, and after the first call the server hands out a small integer nickname so the client need not resend its full credentials.

A server checks that each timestamp is greater than the previous one from that client and has not passed the credential's window, which acts as a lifetime. These checks guard against replayed requests.
sections.eli5: It is like showing an ID card. The server can accept a plain claim, a card with your name, or a secret handshake with a clock check so nobody can copy your old note.

sections.title: Transports and Record Marking
sections.content:
RPC does not care how a message gets from one process to another, and it does not implement reliability. On a reliable transport such as TCP, a reply tells the application the procedure ran exactly once, but a missing reply tells it nothing, and timeouts and reconnection are still needed after server crashes. On an unreliable transport such as UDP, the application must supply its own timeouts, retransmission and duplicate detection. If it retransmits and gets a reply, it can only infer the procedure ran at least once.

A server can approximate execute-at-most-once behaviour by remembering the xid of calls it has executed and skipping repeats. It may use the xid only to test for equality.

When messages ride a byte stream such as TCP, the RFC defines record marking to separate them. One RPC message fits in one record, and a record is made of fragments. Each fragment has a four-byte header: the highest-order bit says whether this is the last fragment, and the other 31 bits give the fragment's length in bytes.

The RFC also notes two uses beyond ordinary calls. In batching, the client sends many calls without waiting and the server sends no replies. In broadcast RPC, a client sends one call and waits for many replies.
sections.eli5: RPC only writes the notes. If the post is unreliable, you must resend lost notes yourself. On a pipe of continuous bytes, each note gets a small size tag so the reader knows where it ends.

sections.title: The Port Mapper
sections.content:
Appendix A defines the port mapper, which maps an RPC program number, version and transport protocol to a port number. Reserved port numbers are scarce and remote programs are many, so only the port mapper runs on a fixed port, 111. Other programs register there when they start, and clients ask it where to find a program.

Its procedures are PMAPPROC_NULL (0), PMAPPROC_SET (1), PMAPPROC_UNSET (2), PMAPPROC_GETPORT (3), PMAPPROC_DUMP (4) and PMAPPROC_CALLIT (5). The port mapper itself is program number 100000, version 2, reachable over UDP or TCP. PMAPPROC_SET refuses to create a mapping that already exists for the same program, version and protocol. GETPORT returns zero if the program is not registered.

PMAPPROC_CALLIT supports broadcast. The client sends the call to the port mapper at the broadcast address, each port mapper calls its local service, and it replies only if the call succeeded. It talks to the local program over UDP only.

Section 11 adds the RPC language, an extension of XDR with program, version and procedure declarations. By convention, procedure 0 of any RPC protocol takes no arguments, returns nothing and needs no authentication.
sections.eli5: The port mapper is the front desk with a fixed number. You ask it which room a helper is in, then go there.

items.desc: Remote cannot support the version number.

items.desc: No identity; the server does not care who calls.

items.desc: UNIX-style user and group IDs; no real verifier.
